note: Authored Security+ SY0-701 questions. Every distractor is an adjacent objective-list term or a true-but-broader real-world word; every explanation names the discriminator rather than restating the definition. Generated by tools/build-bank.mjs from tools/authored/ — edit the source files, not this.

items.objective: 1.1 Compare and contrast various types of security controls.
items.stem: A company posts signs at the perimeter reading "This area is under 24-hour video surveillance." The signs are not connected to any system. Which control TYPE do the signs represent?
items.explanation: The binary test is whether it can actually stop someone. A sign cannot. Deterrent discourages before the fact; preventive physically or logically blocks. The cameras themselves would be detective — they record but do not intervene.

items.objective: 1.1 Compare and contrast various types of security controls.
items.stem: An organisation cannot deploy multifactor authentication on a legacy application, so it restricts access to a single hardened jump host and logs every session. What is the jump host acting as?
items.explanation: Compensating is specifically the control you put in when the control you wanted is not feasible. Corrective repairs damage after an event has already happened — nothing has happened here.

items.objective: 1.1 Compare and contrast various types of security controls.
items.stem: Which of the following is a MANAGERIAL control?
items.explanation: Category asks what kind of thing it is. Managerial is the paperwork that governs — policy, planning, risk assessment. The guard is operational (a person, day to day), the cabinet physical, the firewall technical.

items.objective: 1.1 Compare and contrast various types of security controls.
items.stem: Security awareness training delivered to all staff each quarter is BEST classified as which control category?
items.explanation: Operational controls are executed by people as part of running the business. The policy that requires the training is managerial; the training session itself is operational. This pair is the most common category mix-up.

items.objective: 1.1 Compare and contrast various types of security controls.
items.stem: After a ransomware incident, the team restores affected servers from backup. Restoring from backup is which control type?
items.explanation: Corrective controls repair damage after an event. "Recovery" feels right because it is an incident response phase — but it is not one of the six control types, which are preventive, deterrent, detective, corrective, compensating and directive.

items.objective: 1.1 Compare and contrast various types of security controls.
items.stem: An acceptable use policy that states employees must not install unapproved software is BEST described as which control type?
items.explanation: Directive controls tell people what they must do. Managerial is a valid description but it answers the CATEGORY question, not the TYPE question — read which of the two lists the stem is asking for.

items.objective: 1.1 Compare and contrast various types of security controls.
items.stem: A firewall configured to drop traffic from known-malicious IP addresses is BEST classified as which combination?
items.explanation: It blocks the traffic, so it is preventive rather than detective; it is enforced by a machine, so it is technical rather than operational. This exact pairing is the canonical Security+ classification question.

items.objective: 1.1 Compare and contrast various types of security controls.
items.stem: A bollard installed outside a data centre entrance is which control CATEGORY and TYPE?
items.explanation: A bollard physically stops a vehicle, so preventive rather than deterrent. Category is physical because it is a barrier rather than a machine, a person or a document.

items.objective: 1.2 Summarize fundamental security concepts.
items.stem: A contract must be signed digitally so that the signer cannot later deny having signed it. Which security concept does this requirement describe?
items.explanation: Integrity proves the document did not change. Non-repudiation proves WHO acted and removes their ability to deny it. The mechanism is a digital signature — reaching for encryption here is the classic upgrade error.

items.objective: 1.2 Summarize fundamental security concepts.
items.stem: An attacker modifies the account number in a payment file while it is in transit. Which element of the CIA triad has been violated?
items.explanation: Integrity is the assurance data has not been altered. Confidentiality would be violated by reading the file; availability by preventing access to it. Non-repudiation is not part of the triad.

items.objective: 1.2 Summarize fundamental security concepts.
items.stem: In a Zero Trust architecture, which component evaluates policy and makes the decision to grant or deny a request?
items.explanation: The Policy Engine decides. The Policy Administrator communicates and executes that decision. Both are Control Plane. The Enforcement Point, on the Data Plane, is what actually allows or blocks the traffic.

items.objective: 1.2 Summarize fundamental security concepts.
items.stem: Which Zero Trust component sits in the traffic path and actually permits or blocks the connection?
items.explanation: The Policy Enforcement Point is the only one of the three "policy" components on the DATA plane. Engine and Administrator are Control Plane. That split is the most-tested Zero Trust distinction in Domain 1.

items.objective: 1.2 Summarize fundamental security concepts.
items.stem: A Zero Trust design limits what any single compromised credential can reach. Which Control Plane concept does the objectives document use for this?
items.explanation: Least privilege and segmentation are real terms but they belong to objectives 2.5 and 4.6. Inside Zero Trust's Control Plane the objectives word is threat scope reduction. The objective you are in decides the credited word.

items.objective: 1.2 Summarize fundamental security concepts.
items.stem: An organisation compares its current controls against the ISO 27001 control set to see what is missing before starting certification. What is this activity called?
items.explanation: Gap analysis measures the present state against a chosen target standard. A risk assessment measures exposure to threats — it does not need a standard to compare against.

items.objective: 1.2 Summarize fundamental security concepts.
items.stem: Security places a document named "executive_salaries_2026.xlsx" on a file share. It contains nothing real, and opening it raises an alert. What is this?
items.explanation: Scale is the discriminator: honeytoken is one record or credential, honeyfile is one file, honeypot is a whole system, honeynet is a network of honeypots.

items.objective: 1.2 Summarize fundamental security concepts.
items.stem: A fake set of database credentials is planted that no application uses. Any authentication attempt with them triggers an immediate alert. What is this called?
items.explanation: A honeytoken is data that should never legitimately be USED — credentials, an API key, a record. A honeyfile is data that should never legitimately be OPENED.

items.objective: 1.2 Summarize fundamental security concepts.
items.stem: A facility uses two interlocking doors where the second will not open until the first has closed, preventing tailgating. Which objective-list term describes this?
items.explanation: Mantrap is the traditional industry word and is deliberately not on the SY0-701 list. When real-world usage and the objectives disagree, answer with the objectives.

items.objective: 1.2 Summarize fundamental security concepts.
items.stem: Which physical security control is specifically intended to stop a vehicle from reaching a building entrance?
items.explanation: Bollards are vehicle-specific. Fencing defines a perimeter against people. Both are on the 1.2 physical security list, and the stem naming a vehicle is the discriminator.

items.objective: 1.2 Summarize fundamental security concepts.
items.stem: A sensor detects an intruder by measuring the reflection of high-frequency sound waves off a moving body. Which sensor type is this?
items.explanation: Ultrasonic uses sound; microwave uses radio energy; infrared detects heat; pressure detects weight. The objectives list all four and questions distinguish them by the physical phenomenon named.

items.objective: 1.2 Summarize fundamental security concepts.
items.stem: Which AAA function answers the question "what did this user actually do while logged in"?
items.explanation: Authentication is who you are, authorization is what you may do, accounting is the record of what you did. Attestation is a 4.6/5.5 term about confirming something is valid, not part of AAA.

items.objective: 1.3 Explain the importance of change management processes and the impact to security.
items.stem: A change request is rejected because it does not document how the change would be reversed if it fails. Which element is missing?
items.explanation: A backout plan is scoped to one change. A disaster recovery plan is scoped to the whole site or service and is a 5.1 policy, not a change-management artifact.

items.objective: 1.3 Explain the importance of change management processes and the impact to security.
items.stem: A change board approves a database upgrade to run between 02:00 and 04:00 on Sunday. What is that agreed period called?
items.explanation: The maintenance window is the PERMISSION to cause disruption; downtime is the CONSEQUENCE. The objectives list both separately and questions trade on the difference.

items.objective: 1.3 Explain the importance of change management processes and the impact to security.
items.stem: Before approving a firewall rule change, the team documents which business services would be affected and how badly. What is this step?
items.explanation: Impact analysis assesses consequences before approval. Test results are the evidence you bring to that approval — they show the change works, not what it would break.

items.objective: 1.3 Explain the importance of change management processes and the impact to security.
items.stem: A configuration management system retains every previous revision of a firewall ruleset so any version can be restored. Which 1.3 element is this?
items.explanation: Version control is the artifact that records what the file looked like before. Change management is the surrounding process. The backout plan is the intent to revert; version control is what makes reverting possible.

items.objective: 1.3 Explain the importance of change management processes and the impact to security.
items.stem: An upgrade is blocked because a critical in-house application will not run on the new operating system version. Which technical implication does this illustrate?
items.explanation: The blocker is an old application that cannot move. Dependencies would apply if the change required another change first, or if a service relied on this one — the constraint here is the application's age, not an ordering relationship.

items.objective: 1.4 Explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions.
items.stem: A random value is added to each password before it is hashed, so that two users with the same password produce different stored hashes. What is this called?
items.explanation: Salting defeats precomputed rainbow tables by making each hash unique. Key stretching is the different defence of making each individual guess slow — it attacks the attacker's time, not their precomputation.

items.objective: 1.4 Explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions.
items.stem: A password storage scheme deliberately applies thousands of hashing iterations so that each guess is computationally expensive. What is this technique called?
items.explanation: Key stretching increases the cost per attempt. Salting makes each hash unique. Both are used together in PBKDF2 and bcrypt, and questions test which one addresses which attack.

items.objective: 1.4 Explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions.
items.stem: A payment system replaces each card number with a randomly generated reference. The real number is held in a separate secured vault. What is this?
items.explanation: Tokenization removes the real value from the system entirely and is reversible through the vault. Masking leaves the real value in place and only hides characters on display.

items.objective: 1.4 Explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions.
items.stem: A support application displays a customer's card number as ************4471. The full number remains in the database. Which technique is this?
items.explanation: Masking is a display control — the real value is still underneath. If the real value had left the system and been replaced by a meaningless reference, it would be tokenization.

items.objective: 1.4 Explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions.
items.stem: An insider exfiltrates a document by embedding it in the pixel data of a holiday photograph posted to social media. Which technique is this?
items.explanation: Encryption hides the MEANING and is obvious — anyone can see there is ciphertext. Steganography hides the EXISTENCE, so it looks like nothing happened at all.

items.objective: 1.4 Explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions.
items.stem: A laptop stores its full-disk encryption key in a dedicated chip soldered to the motherboard, which will release it only if boot integrity checks pass. What is the chip?
items.explanation: A TPM is one chip bound to one machine. An HSM is a separate appliance serving many systems — the discriminator is whether the device belongs to one host or to the estate.

items.objective: 1.4 Explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions.
items.stem: A payment processor needs a tamper-resistant appliance to generate and store keys for thousands of transactions per second across many servers. Which tool fits?
items.explanation: Scale and independence from any one host make it an HSM. A TPM would be tied to a single machine and could not serve the fleet.

items.objective: 1.4 Explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions.
items.stem: A browser needs to check whether one specific certificate has been revoked, without downloading a large list. Which mechanism does this?
items.explanation: OCSP is a live query about one certificate. A CRL is a published list you download in full. Same purpose, opposite mechanism — the stem's "one specific certificate, without a large list" is the tell.

items.objective: 1.4 Explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions.
items.stem: An administrator generates a key pair and produces a file containing the public key and organisation details to send to a certificate authority. What is that file?
items.explanation: You generate the CSR; the CA signs it and returns the certificate. The request is not the authority and is not yet a certificate.

items.objective: 1.4 Explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions.
items.stem: A company needs one certificate that will secure mail.example.com, vpn.example.com and any future host under example.com. Which certificate type fits?
items.explanation: A wildcard covers *.example.com including hosts that do not exist yet. A Subject Alternative Name certificate lists specific names and would need reissuing for a new host — and SAN is in the acronym list, not the 1.4 bullet list.

items.objective: 1.4 Explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions.
items.stem: A regulator requires that a copy of each employee's private key be recoverable by the organisation if the employee leaves. What is this arrangement?
items.explanation: Escrow is about who ELSE holds a copy of the key. A key management system is the tooling that issues, rotates and retires keys — it is where escrow would be implemented, not the concept itself.

items.objective: 1.4 Explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions.
items.stem: Two parties who have never communicated before need to agree a shared secret over an untrusted network. Which cryptographic operation accomplishes this?
items.explanation: Key exchange establishes a shared symmetric key over an insecure channel — Diffie-Hellman is the classic example. Signatures prove origin; hashing proves integrity; neither creates a shared secret.

items.objective: 1.4 Explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions.
items.stem: An organisation encrypts a specific column of customer identifiers rather than the whole storage volume. Which encryption LEVEL is in use?
items.explanation: The objectives list six levels from full-disk down to record. Encrypting individual rows or fields is record-level; database-level would protect the whole database instance uniformly.

items.objective: 1.4 Explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions.
items.stem: A distributed ledger records transactions in linked blocks that any participant can verify and none can retroactively alter. Which 1.4 terms BEST describe this?
items.explanation: The objectives list blockchain and open public ledger as adjacent terms in 1.4. Hashing is the primitive that makes the chain tamper-evident, but the structure itself is the blockchain.

items.objective: 1.4 Explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions.
items.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes symmetric from asymmetric encryption?
options: Symmetric uses one shared key; asymmetric uses a public/private key pair
Symmetric uses a key pair; asymmetric uses one shared key
Symmetric is used only for signatures; asymmetric only for bulk data
Symmetric cannot be used over a network; asymmetric can
items.explanation: One key both directions is symmetric (AES). A mathematically related pair is asymmetric (RSA, ECC). Because asymmetric is slow, real systems use it to exchange a symmetric key and then encrypt the bulk data symmetrically.

items.objective: 1.4 Explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions.
items.stem: A hardware root of trust is BEST described as which of the following?
options: The certificate authority at the top of a PKI hierarchy
A component inherently trusted to anchor the verification of everything above it
A list of certificates that have been revoked
A backup copy of the private key held by a third party
items.explanation: Root of trust is the anchor that verification chains back to and that cannot itself be verified by anything else. A root CA is one example of the idea, but the objectives list root of trust as its own term.

items.objective: 2.1 Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations.
items.stem: A marketing team signs up for an unapproved SaaS analytics platform and uploads customer data, because procurement was taking too long. Which threat actor category does the objectives document use?
items.explanation: Insider threat implies intent to harm. Shadow IT is well-meaning and still appears on CompTIA's threat actor list — that is exactly why it is easy to miss.

items.objective: 2.1 Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations.
items.stem: An attacker downloads a ready-made exploit kit and runs it without understanding how it works. Which SY0-701 term describes this actor?
items.explanation: Script kiddie is the traditional word and is deliberately absent from SY0-701. When real-world usage and the objectives disagree, answer with the objectives.

items.objective: 2.1 Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations.
items.stem: A group breaches a chemical company and leaks internal documents to protest its environmental record. Which motivation BEST fits?
items.explanation: The motivation list separates having a cause from simply wanting to break things. A stated protest means philosophical/political beliefs; disruption/chaos is damage for its own sake.

items.objective: 2.1 Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations.
items.stem: A state-sponsored group maintains covert access to a defence contractor for two years, collecting design documents without disrupting anything. Which motivation applies?
items.explanation: Espionage steals in order to KNOW, over time and covertly. Data exfiltration is the broader act of moving data out — it describes the mechanism, while espionage describes the purpose the stem gives.

items.objective: 2.1 Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations.
items.stem: A security researcher discovers a flaw and reports it to the vendor rather than exploiting it. Which motivation does the objectives document list for this?
items.explanation: Ethical is a motivation on CompTIA's list and is routinely forgotten by people reproducing the list from intuition, because it does not feel like an attacker motivation at all.

items.objective: 2.1 Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations.
items.stem: Which attribute BEST distinguishes a nation-state actor from organized crime?
options: Whether the actor is internal or external
Whether the actor is motivated by money
items.explanation: The three attributes the objectives list are internal/external, resources/funding and level of sophistication/capability. Both actors are external and both may seek money; only funding and sophistication separate them reliably.

items.objective: 2.1 Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations.
items.stem: A recently dismissed administrator uses credentials that were never revoked to delete production backups. Which combination BEST describes this?
options: Organized crime motivated by financial gain
Unskilled attacker motivated by ethical concerns
items.explanation: The actor had legitimate access, which makes them an insider threat; dismissal followed by destruction points to revenge rather than gain. Shadow IT is never malicious by definition.

items.objective: 2.2 Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces.
items.stem: An attacker registers "exarnple.com" — an "rn" in place of the "m" — and hosts a copy of a bank's login page. Which threat vector is the domain registration itself?
items.explanation: Typosquatting is specifically about the DOMAIN NAME being a near-miss. Brand impersonation is about the content looking like the company — the copied login page is brand impersonation; the domain is typosquatting.

items.objective: 2.2 Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces.
items.stem: A caller tells the help desk they are the new regional auditor and needs a password reset before a board meeting in ten minutes. Which technique is the invented backstory?
items.explanation: Pretexting is the invented STORY that makes the request plausible. Impersonation is claiming to be a specific real person. The phone as the channel makes it vishing — the objectives list all three separately.

items.objective: 2.2 Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces.
items.stem: An accounts payable clerk receives an email from the CEO's genuine-looking address instructing an urgent supplier payment to a new bank account. Which term BEST fits?
items.explanation: BEC targets a specific business process using a trusted internal identity. Plain phishing is the broad net cast at many recipients — the specificity of the target and the process is the discriminator.

items.objective: 2.2 Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces.
items.stem: Attackers compromise an industry association website that engineers at a target company read daily, and serve malware from it. Which vector is this?
items.explanation: Watering hole compromises a site the victims VISIT. Supply chain compromises something they BUY or INSTALL. The binary test is whether the malicious thing entered through browsing or through procurement.

items.objective: 2.2 Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces.
items.stem: An employee receives a text message claiming a parcel is held and linking to a payment page. Which vector is this?
items.explanation: S for SMS, V for voice. The objectives also list Short Message Service (SMS) as a message-based vector in its own right, but the social engineering technique is smishing.

items.objective: 2.2 Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces.
items.stem: A vulnerability scan finds a development server exposing an unauthenticated database listener that no application uses. Which 2.2 attack surface does this represent?
items.explanation: Open service ports is the 2.2 attack SURFACE. Misconfiguration is a 2.3 VULNERABILITY. Both are defensible in plain English — the objective the question sits in decides which word is credited.

items.objective: 2.2 Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces.
items.stem: An organisation discovers that a managed service provider with remote access to its network has been breached, and the attacker pivoted inward. Which vector is this?
items.explanation: The objectives list MSPs, vendors and suppliers under supply chain. The attacker entered through a trusted third party you contracted with, not through something staff visited.

items.objective: 2.2 Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces.
items.stem: A new network appliance is deployed and reachable with the credentials printed in its manual. Which threat vector is this?
items.explanation: Default credentials is its own bullet in 2.2 and the corresponding hardening technique in 2.5 is "default password changes". Naming both halves is a common question pattern.

items.objective: 2.2 Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces.
items.stem: Malware is delivered inside a QR code printed on a poster in a building lobby. Which threat vector does the objectives document use for this delivery method?
items.explanation: The objectives list image-based as a vector alongside file-based and message-based. A QR code is an image that carries the payload or destination.

items.objective: 2.3 Explain various types of vulnerabilities.
items.stem: An application checks that a file is owned by the user, then opens it. An attacker replaces the file between those two operations. Which vulnerability class is this?
items.explanation: Any gap between the check and the use is a race condition — the objectives name the two halves time-of-check (TOC) and time-of-use (TOU). If a stem describes timing between two operations, this is the answer.

items.objective: 2.3 Explain various types of vulnerabilities.
items.stem: A guest virtual machine exploits a hypervisor flaw to run code directly on the host. Which vulnerability is this?
items.explanation: Escape crosses the isolation boundary. Resource reuse is the different problem of memory or storage being handed to a new tenant with the previous tenant's data still present.

items.objective: 2.3 Explain various types of vulnerabilities.
items.stem: A cloud provider allocates a block of storage to a new customer without wiping it, and the previous customer's data is readable. Which vulnerability is this?
items.explanation: Resource reuse is specifically the failure to sanitise a shared resource between tenants. Nothing crossed an isolation boundary by force, which is what would make it an escape.

items.objective: 2.3 Explain various types of vulnerabilities.
items.stem: A user installs an application package obtained from a website rather than the device's official app store. Which mobile vulnerability is this?
items.explanation: Side loading installs one app AROUND the store while the OS restrictions remain. Jailbreaking removes those restrictions entirely — the discriminator is whether the platform's protections were defeated or merely bypassed for one install.

items.objective: 2.3 Explain various types of vulnerabilities.
items.stem: A vulnerability is being actively exploited and the vendor has not yet released a fix because they only learned of it today. What is this?
items.explanation: Zero-day means no patch exists YET. End-of-life means no patch will EVER come because support has ended. Both leave you unpatched; only one can be fixed by waiting.

items.objective: 2.3 Explain various types of vulnerabilities.
items.stem: An organisation continues running a database server whose vendor stopped issuing security updates two years ago. Which hardware/software vulnerability applies?
items.explanation: End-of-life is the permanent condition of no further patches. The related consideration in 3.1 is "inability to patch" — the same situation viewed as an architecture trade-off.

items.objective: 2.3 Explain various types of vulnerabilities.
items.stem: Attackers compromise a software vendor's build pipeline so that a digitally signed update distributes a backdoor. Which 2.3 application vulnerability does the objectives document name?
items.explanation: Malicious update is listed explicitly under Application vulnerabilities. Supply chain also appears in 2.3, but when the update MECHANISM is the vector the objectives give you a more specific word — use it.

items.objective: 2.3 Explain various types of vulnerabilities.
items.stem: A web application concatenates user input directly into a database query, allowing an attacker to return all rows of a table. Which vulnerability is this?
items.explanation: SQLi manipulates the DATABASE QUERY. XSS injects script that runs in another user's BROWSER. The target of the injected content is the discriminator.

items.objective: 2.3 Explain various types of vulnerabilities.
items.stem: An attacker stores a script in a forum post so that it executes in the browser of every subsequent visitor. Which vulnerability is this?
items.explanation: XSS executes in another user's browser and targets the site's visitors. SQLi targets the database. Both are listed under 2.3 web-based vulnerabilities and are separated by where the injected content runs.

items.objective: 2.3 Explain various types of vulnerabilities.
items.stem: An IoT camera runs an embedded operating system whose vendor ships updates only as full binary images, and none have been released since launch. Which 2.3 hardware vulnerability is MOST directly named?
items.explanation: The objectives list firmware, end-of-life and legacy under Hardware. The stem points at the embedded software image itself, which is firmware.

items.objective: 2.4 Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity.
items.stem: Malware spreads across the network to hundreds of hosts without any user opening a file. Which malware type is this?
items.explanation: A worm self-propagates. A virus needs a host file and a user to run it. A trojan needs the user to run it believing it is something else. Autonomy is the discriminator.

items.objective: 2.4 Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity.
items.stem: A departing developer leaves code in a payroll system that deletes records if their employee ID stops appearing in the staff table. Which malware type is this?
items.explanation: A logic bomb is defined by its TRIGGER — a date, an event, a condition. A trojan is defined by DISGUISE. Nothing here is pretending to be something else; it is waiting for a condition.

items.objective: 2.4 Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity.
items.stem: Malware modifies operating system kernel structures so that its own processes and files do not appear in any listing. Which type is this?
items.explanation: A rootkit is defined by CONCEALMENT at a privileged level. Spyware is defined by what it collects. Malware can be both — the stem here describes only the hiding.

items.objective: 2.4 Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity.
items.stem: New laptops arrive with trial software and vendor utilities nobody requested, increasing the attack surface. Which term does SY0-701 use?
items.explanation: PUP is the industry word and appears only in the acronym list. Bloatware is the 2.4 malware bullet, and it is the credited answer.

items.objective: 2.4 Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity.
items.stem: An attacker tries the single password "Autumn2026!" against every account in the directory, once each. Which password attack is this?
items.explanation: Spraying is wide and shallow — one password across many accounts, specifically to stay under lockout thresholds. Brute force is deep against one account and triggers lockout quickly.

items.objective: 2.4 Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity.
items.stem: A researcher demonstrates two different files that produce an identical SHA-1 digest. What is the RESULT called?
items.explanation: A collision is the RESULT — two inputs, one hash. A birthday attack is the probability METHOD used to find one efficiently. The stem asks what the outcome is called.

items.objective: 2.4 Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity.
items.stem: An on-path attacker strips the TLS 1.3 offer from a handshake so the session negotiates an obsolete cipher suite. Which cryptographic attack is this?
items.explanation: On-path is the POSITION the attacker holds; downgrade is what they DO from it. The question asks for the cryptographic attack, so the position alone is not the answer.

items.objective: 2.4 Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity.
items.stem: A single account authenticates from London at 09:14 and from São Paulo at 09:31. Which indicator is this?
items.explanation: Impossible travel is about GEOGRAPHY versus elapsed time. Concurrent session usage is two live sessions regardless of location — it would apply even if both were in the same building.

items.objective: 2.4 Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity.
items.stem: A nightly batch job normally writes its log at 23:00. Entries now appear at 04:00 as well. Which indicator does the objectives document name?
items.explanation: Out-of-cycle logging means the log EXISTS but at the wrong time. Missing logs means it is not there at all. Questions trade on which of the two the stem actually describes.

items.objective: 2.4 Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity.
items.stem: Investigating a suspected breach, an analyst finds that the security event log on a server is empty for the three days around the intrusion. Which indicator is this?
items.explanation: Absence is itself the indicator — logs that should exist and do not. This is one of the nine named indicators, and clearing logs is a standard anti-forensic step.

items.objective: 2.4 Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity.
items.stem: A DDoS attack sends small DNS queries with a spoofed source address to open resolvers, which return much larger responses to the victim. Which characteristic does "much larger responses" describe?
items.explanation: Reflected means the response goes to the SPOOFED victim rather than the sender. Amplified means the response is far LARGER than the request. This attack is both, but the stem asks about the size multiplier.

items.objective: 2.4 Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity.
items.stem: A web application accepts a filename parameter and an attacker submits ../../../etc/passwd to read a system file. Which application attack is this?
items.explanation: Directory traversal escapes the intended PATH. Injection inserts code or query syntax into an interpreter. Nothing is being executed here — a file outside the web root is simply being read.

items.objective: 2.4 Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity.
items.stem: An attacker captures a Kerberos ticket from the network and presents it later to authenticate as that user. Which network attack does the objectives document name?
items.explanation: The objectives list "Replay" under application attacks and "Credential replay" under network attacks. Because what was captured and reused is authentication material, credential replay is the matching bullet.

items.objective: 2.4 Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity.
items.stem: An attacker clones the identifier from an employee badge by reading it from a short distance in a lift. Which physical attack is this?
items.explanation: RFID cloning is listed under physical attacks in 2.4. Brute force in that same list means physically forcing a door or barrier, not guessing a password.

items.objective: 2.4 Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity.
items.stem: An attacker deliberately raises the temperature in a server room by tampering with HVAC controls until systems shut down. Which physical attack category applies?
items.explanation: Environmental attacks manipulate the conditions systems depend on — power, cooling, water. Resource consumption is an INDICATOR you would observe, and service disruption is a 2.1 motivation, not an attack type.

items.objective: 2.4 Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity.
items.stem: A standard user exploits an unpatched local flaw to obtain SYSTEM-level rights on a workstation. Which application attack is this?
items.explanation: Privilege escalation is gaining rights beyond those assigned. It is listed under application attacks in 2.4, and the discriminator is that the attacker already had some access and increased it.

items.objective: 2.5 Explain the purpose of mitigation techniques used to secure the enterprise.
items.stem: To limit lateral movement, a network is divided into zones with filtering between them so a compromise in one cannot reach the others. Which mitigation is this?
items.explanation: Segmentation divides the network into zones. Isolation cuts one host off entirely. The stem describes a structural division of the whole network, not the removal of a single machine.

items.objective: 2.5 Explain the purpose of mitigation techniques used to secure the enterprise.
items.stem: Workstations are configured so that only executables on an approved list may run, and everything else is blocked by default. Which mitigation is this?
items.explanation: Application allow list names the specific permitted software. Configuration enforcement is the different control of making settings stick and revert if changed.

items.objective: 2.5 Explain the purpose of mitigation techniques used to secure the enterprise.
items.stem: A retired file server is formally removed from service, its data destroyed and its entries deleted from the asset register. Which 2.5 mitigation is this?
items.explanation: Decommissioning is the 2.5 process for retiring a system. Sanitization is the 4.2 disposal step INSIDE it that destroys the data. The stem describes the whole retirement, not just the wipe.

items.objective: 2.5 Explain the purpose of mitigation techniques used to secure the enterprise.
items.stem: Which hardening technique does the objectives document name for closing services a server does not need to expose?
items.explanation: Disabling ports/protocols turns off the listening service. Removal of unnecessary software takes the package off the machine entirely — one closes a door, the other removes the room.

items.objective: 2.5 Explain the purpose of mitigation techniques used to secure the enterprise.
items.stem: An endpoint is configured to inspect and block malicious behaviour locally, on the host itself, rather than at the network boundary. Which hardening technique does the objectives document name?
items.explanation: HIPS is named explicitly in the 2.5 hardening list and it BLOCKS. A host-based firewall filters connections rather than behaviour; endpoint protection is the broader antimalware category.

items.objective: 2.5 Explain the purpose of mitigation techniques used to secure the enterprise.
items.stem: A helpdesk technician's account is changed so it can reset passwords but no longer create domain administrators. Which mitigation does this apply?
items.explanation: Least privilege is the principle of granting only what the role needs. Permissions and ACLs are the mechanisms that express it — the stem describes the principle being applied by reducing rights to the task.

items.objective: 3.1 Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models.
items.stem: Before migrating, a team documents which security tasks the cloud provider performs and which remain the customer's. What is this document called?
items.explanation: The responsibility matrix divides DUTIES. An SLA commits to PERFORMANCE and is a 5.3 agreement type. Both are cloud contract documents and questions swap them deliberately.

items.objective: 3.1 Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models.
items.stem: A team defines its entire cloud environment in declarative template files held in a Git repository and applied by a pipeline. Which 3.1 concept is this?
items.explanation: IaC is the 3.1 architecture term for infrastructure defined in version-controlled files. Automation is the 4.7 benefit you get from it — the objective the question sits in decides the credited word.

items.objective: 3.1 Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models.
items.stem: A control system is kept on a network with no physical connection of any kind to any other network. Which term applies?
items.explanation: Air gap is PHYSICAL isolation — no cable, no wireless. Logical segmentation is VLANs and routing rules on shared hardware, which can be misconfigured; an air gap cannot.

items.objective: 3.1 Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models.
items.stem: An application is split into independently deployable components that communicate over APIs, each owning its own data. Which architecture is this?
items.explanation: Microservices is about how the APPLICATION is decomposed. Containerization is a packaging and runtime technology often used to deploy them — the stem describes the decomposition, not the packaging.

items.objective: 3.1 Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models.
items.stem: Several workloads share a single operating system kernel while remaining isolated from each other. Which technology is this?
items.explanation: Containers share the host KERNEL; virtual machines each carry a full guest OS. That single sentence is the discriminator, and it is why container escape and VM escape are different risks.

items.objective: 3.1 Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models.
items.stem: A manufacturing plant runs equipment controllers that must respond to inputs within guaranteed, fixed time limits. Which architecture does the objectives document name?
items.explanation: RTOS is defined by the GUARANTEED TIMING requirement. Embedded systems is the broader category of purpose-built computers; ICS/SCADA is the industrial control application layer above.

items.objective: 3.1 Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models.
items.stem: An organisation buys cyber insurance to cover the cost of a potential breach. Which 3.1 architecture consideration does this illustrate?
items.explanation: Risk transference moves the financial loss to another party. It appears in 3.1 as an architecture consideration and again in 5.2 as the "Transfer" risk management strategy — the same idea in two objectives.

items.objective: 3.1 Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models.
items.stem: A medical device runs a fixed software image that the manufacturer will not permit the hospital to modify, and no updates are offered. Which 3.1 consideration does this MOST directly raise?
items.explanation: The objectives list both. Patch availability asks whether a patch EXISTS; inability to patch is the stronger condition that you cannot apply one even if it does. The stem says modification is not permitted.

items.objective: 3.1 Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models.
items.stem: Code runs on demand in response to events, with the provider managing all underlying compute. Which model is this?
items.explanation: Serverless removes the server you manage — you supply only the function. Servers still exist; the point is that patching and capacity are no longer in your responsibility column of the matrix.

items.objective: 3.1 Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models.
items.stem: Which security implication is the MOST significant difference between a centralized and a decentralized architecture?
options: Centralized offers consistent policy enforcement but is a larger single point of failure
Decentralized is always more secure because there is no single target
Centralized cannot use encryption in transit
Decentralized removes the need for identity management
items.explanation: The trade-off is uniformity against blast radius. Decentralized spreads risk but makes consistent policy harder — neither is inherently more secure, which is why the objectives list it as a comparison.

items.objective: 3.2 Given a scenario, apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure.
items.stem: Administrators must connect to a single hardened host, and only from there can they reach production servers. What is that host called?
items.explanation: You log INTO a jump server and work from it. A proxy forwards traffic on your behalf and you never authenticate to it as a shell. The stem says administrators connect to it, then onward.

items.objective: 3.2 Given a scenario, apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure.
items.stem: A network appliance receives a copy of traffic from a switch port and analyses it without sitting in the forwarding path. Which device attribute describes this placement?
items.explanation: Inline versus tap/monitor is about PLACEMENT in the traffic path. Active versus passive is about whether the device can ACT on what it sees. Questions swap these two axes deliberately.

items.objective: 3.2 Given a scenario, apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure.
items.stem: A security appliance is configured so that if it crashes, all traffic is blocked until it recovers. Which failure mode is this?
items.explanation: Fail-closed favours security at the cost of availability; fail-open favours availability at the cost of security. Name the property the scenario chose to protect.

items.objective: 3.2 Given a scenario, apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure.
items.stem: Which standard authenticates a device at the switch port before granting it any network access?
items.explanation: 802.1X is the 3.2 port security standard. EAP is the authentication framework carried inside it, RADIUS is the back-end server, and NAC is the broader 4.5 enterprise capability built on top.

items.objective: 3.2 Given a scenario, apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure.
items.stem: An organisation wants SD-WAN connectivity combined with cloud-delivered secure web gateway, CASB and Zero Trust access in a single service. Which term describes this?
items.explanation: SD-WAN is the networking alone. SASE is SD-WAN with the security stack folded in and delivered from the cloud edge. The stem lists security services on top of connectivity, which is the SASE definition.

items.objective: 3.2 Given a scenario, apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure.
items.stem: Which device inspects HTTP requests specifically to block SQL injection and cross-site scripting before they reach an application?
items.explanation: A WAF understands ONE protocol deeply and is placed in front of a specific application. An NGFW inspects many protocols and adds identity and application awareness across the estate.

items.objective: 3.2 Given a scenario, apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure.
items.stem: A firewall makes decisions based only on source and destination IP address and port. At which layer is it operating?
items.explanation: Layer 4 filtering uses ports and addresses. Layer 7 understands the application protocol and can distinguish, say, one HTTP method from another. The objectives phrase this pairing as "Layer 4/Layer 7".

items.objective: 3.2 Given a scenario, apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure.
items.stem: An organisation places its public web servers in a separate network segment reachable from the internet but unable to initiate connections into the internal LAN. What is this segment called?
items.explanation: Screened subnet is the objectives' term (4.5, under Firewall) for what used to be called a DMZ. Security zone is the more general 3.2 concept of which a screened subnet is one instance.

items.objective: 3.2 Given a scenario, apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure.
items.stem: Remote workers connect through an encrypted tunnel that carries all their traffic back to the corporate network. Which secure communication method is this?
items.explanation: A VPN creates the encrypted tunnel. Tunneling protocols named in the objectives are TLS and IPSec — the VPN is the service, those are the mechanisms.

items.objective: 3.3 Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data.
items.stem: Customer records are currently loaded into an application server's memory and being processed. Which data state is this?
items.explanation: Three states only: at rest on storage, in transit on the network, in use in memory. "Data in motion" is a synonym for in transit and is not the objectives' wording.

items.objective: 3.3 Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data.
items.stem: A company's proprietary manufacturing process is protected commercially by never being published rather than by registration. Which data type is this?
items.explanation: Trade secret is the subset of intellectual property whose value depends entirely on secrecy. Both appear in the 3.3 list, and the discriminator is whether disclosure destroys the value.

items.objective: 3.3 Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data.
items.stem: A European regulator asserts that data held in its jurisdiction is subject to its national law regardless of the owning company's headquarters. Which concept is this?
items.explanation: Sovereignty is the LEGAL consequence of where data sits. Geolocation is simply knowing where it is; geographic restrictions is the control you apply to keep it somewhere.

items.objective: 3.3 Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data.
items.stem: An organisation blocks access to a dataset from any IP address outside its home country. Which method to secure data is this?
items.explanation: Geographic restrictions is the listed CONTROL. Sovereignty is the legal driver that made the control necessary — the stem describes the enforcement, not the reason.

items.objective: 3.3 Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data.
items.stem: Which data classification does the objectives document use for information whose loss would halt core business operations?
items.explanation: The six labels are sensitive, confidential, public, restricted, private and critical. Critical is about operational importance, while the others are largely about who may see it.

items.objective: 3.3 Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data.
items.stem: A log file records events in a format designed for machines to parse and not intended for people to read directly. Which 3.3 data type does the objectives document use?
items.explanation: The objectives pair these as a single bullet. It is one of the easiest terms to miss on a blank-paper reproduction because it does not sound like a classification at all.

items.objective: 3.4 Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture.
items.stem: An alternate facility is fully equipped, holds current replicated data and can take production traffic within minutes. Which site type is this?
items.explanation: Hot is running now with current data. Warm has equipment but needs data restored and time. Cold is space and power only. Time-to-service is the discriminator.

items.objective: 3.4 Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture.
items.stem: A company runs the same critical workload on two different cloud providers so that an outage at one does not stop the service. Which 3.4 concept is this?
items.explanation: Multi-cloud is more than one PROVIDER. Platform diversity is more than one TECHNOLOGY stack — using two different firewall vendors is platform diversity even in one data centre.

items.objective: 3.4 Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture.
items.stem: A database writes a continuous record of every change so that it can be restored to any chosen point in time. Which backup concept is this?
items.explanation: Journaling logs the CHANGES themselves. A snapshot captures the STATE at one moment. Replication continuously copies to another location but does not by itself let you rewind.

items.objective: 3.4 Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture.
items.stem: The incident response team meets in a conference room and talks through their response to a simulated ransomware outbreak. No systems are touched. Which test type is this?
items.explanation: Tabletop is discussion only. Simulation actually exercises the systems or the people. The phrase "no systems are touched" is the discriminator the exam relies on.

items.objective: 3.4 Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture.
items.stem: A disaster recovery test brings up the secondary site and runs it alongside production, comparing outputs without cutting over. Which test type is this?
items.explanation: Parallel processing runs both and compares. Fail over actually switches production to the secondary. The stem explicitly says there is no cutover.

items.objective: 3.4 Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture.
items.stem: Which power component keeps servers running for the few minutes between a mains failure and a generator reaching full output?
items.explanation: A UPS covers the gap using stored energy; a generator sustains the load for hours but takes time to start. The objectives list both, and the discriminator is duration versus immediacy.

items.objective: 3.4 Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture.
items.stem: An organisation assesses whether it will have enough trained responders to sustain a 24-hour incident before it happens. Which 3.4 activity is this?
items.explanation: Capacity planning in the objectives has three named dimensions: people, technology and infrastructure. Headcount is explicitly one of them, which surprises candidates who read capacity as purely technical.

items.objective: 3.4 Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture.
items.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes load balancing from clustering?
options: Load balancing distributes requests across independent nodes; clustering makes several nodes act as one system
Load balancing requires shared storage; clustering does not
Clustering only works in the cloud; load balancing only on premises
They are two names for the same technique
items.explanation: The objectives pair these deliberately as "load balancing vs. clustering". Balancing spreads work across servers that do not know about each other; a cluster presents itself as a single logical system.

items.objective: 4.1 Given a scenario, apply common security techniques to computing resources.
items.stem: An organisation defines the approved starting configuration for all new web servers, deploys it via automation, and audits drift monthly. What is this configuration called?
items.explanation: A secure baseline is yours, and the objectives give it three verbs: establish, deploy, maintain. A benchmark is the EXTERNAL standard (4.4) you measure against, such as a CIS benchmark.

items.objective: 4.1 Given a scenario, apply common security techniques to computing resources.
items.stem: Before installing wireless access points across a new floor, engineers walk the space measuring signal strength and interference. What is this activity called?
items.explanation: The survey is the ACTIVITY; the heat map is the OUTPUT it produces. The objectives list both under wireless installation considerations and questions ask for one while offering the other.

items.objective: 4.1 Given a scenario, apply common security techniques to computing resources.
items.stem: A company purchases and owns all mobile devices but allows employees to use them for personal calls and apps. Which deployment model is this?
items.explanation: COPE: the company buys and owns it, personal use permitted. CYOD: the employee picks from an approved list. BYOD: the employee owns it. Ownership plus who chose it is the discriminator.

items.objective: 4.1 Given a scenario, apply common security techniques to computing resources.
items.stem: Which wireless security standard replaces the WPA2 pre-shared key handshake with Simultaneous Authentication of Equals?
items.explanation: SAE is WPA3's headline change and it defeats offline dictionary attacks against captured handshakes. WPA3 is the only wireless standard named in objective 4.1.

items.objective: 4.1 Given a scenario, apply common security techniques to computing resources.
items.stem: An application rejects any submitted date field that is not in ISO format and any name longer than 64 characters, before processing. Which application security technique is this?
items.explanation: Input validation runs at RUNTIME against data. Static code analysis runs before deployment against source code. Both are 4.1 application security bullets, split by when they act.

items.objective: 4.1 Given a scenario, apply common security techniques to computing resources.
items.stem: A developer applies a cryptographic signature to a compiled application so users can verify it came from the publisher and has not been altered. Which technique is this?
items.explanation: Code signing proves ORIGIN and INTEGRITY of a binary. A plain hash proves integrity only — it cannot tell you who produced the file, because anyone can publish a hash.

items.objective: 4.1 Given a scenario, apply common security techniques to computing resources.
items.stem: A web application sets its session cookie with the Secure and HttpOnly attributes. Which 4.1 application security control is this?
items.explanation: Secure cookies is a named 4.1 bullet. Secure restricts the cookie to HTTPS; HttpOnly hides it from JavaScript, which limits what an XSS flaw can steal.

items.objective: 4.1 Given a scenario, apply common security techniques to computing resources.
items.stem: A suspicious attachment is executed in an isolated, instrumented environment so analysts can watch its behaviour safely. Which technique is this?
items.explanation: Sandboxing exists to OBSERVE safely. Isolation exists to CONTAIN. Quarantine (4.4) is what you do to a file once you have decided it is bad.

items.objective: 4.1 Given a scenario, apply common security techniques to computing resources.
items.stem: Which of the following is named in the objectives as a hardening TARGET rather than a hardening technique?
items.explanation: The 4.1 hardening targets list is the set of THINGS you harden — workstations, switches, routers, servers, ICS/SCADA, embedded systems, RTOS, IoT. The other three options are 2.5 hardening techniques.

items.objective: 4.2 Explain the security implications of proper hardware, software, and data asset management.
items.stem: Decommissioned drives are degaussed and overwritten so no data can be recovered, but the drives are then resold. Which disposal step is this?
items.explanation: Sanitization removes the data but keeps the hardware usable. Destruction makes the hardware unusable. The stem says the drives are resold, which rules out destruction.

items.objective: 4.2 Explain the security implications of proper hardware, software, and data asset management.
items.stem: A disposal vendor provides a signed document confirming which serial numbers were destroyed and by what method. Which 4.2 element is this?
items.explanation: Certification is the 4.2 disposal artifact — proof the destruction happened. Attestation is the 5.4/5.5 compliance statement that a control is in place, a different objective and a different purpose.

items.objective: 4.2 Explain the security implications of proper hardware, software, and data asset management.
items.stem: An organisation runs an automated discovery scan to find every device attached to its networks, including ones not in the asset register. Which activity is this?
items.explanation: The objectives pair inventory and enumeration under monitoring/asset tracking. The inventory is the RECORD you hold; enumeration is the act of DISCOVERING what is actually there.

items.objective: 4.2 Explain the security implications of proper hardware, software, and data asset management.
items.stem: Each new server is assigned a named business owner and a data classification at the point it is commissioned. Which 4.2 activity is this?
items.explanation: The objectives list ownership and classification as the two components of assignment/accounting. Acquisition is the earlier step of buying it; tracking is the ongoing step of knowing where it is.

items.objective: 4.3 Explain various activities associated with vulnerability management.
items.stem: A vulnerability is published with the reference CVE-2026-11842 and a severity of 8.8. Which standard produced the 8.8?
items.explanation: CVE is the IDENTIFIER; CVSS is the SCORE. One names the vulnerability, the other rates it. Questions give you both and ask which produced which.

items.objective: 4.3 Explain various activities associated with vulnerability management.
items.stem: A scanner reports a critical flaw. Manual testing confirms the affected component is not installed. What is the finding?
items.explanation: "Positive" always means the scanner SAID something. A false positive is crying wolf. A false negative is silence where there should have been an alert — the more dangerous of the two.

items.objective: 4.3 Explain various activities associated with vulnerability management.
items.stem: An organisation publishes a policy inviting outside researchers to report flaws safely, and pays them for valid findings. Which term does the objectives document use for the payment element?
items.explanation: Bug bounty sits UNDER responsible disclosure in the objectives and adds the reward. The disclosure programme can exist without any payment at all.

items.objective: 4.3 Explain various activities associated with vulnerability management.
items.stem: A build pipeline checks every third-party library against a database of known vulnerable versions. Which identification method is this?
items.explanation: Package monitoring checks DEPENDENCIES you imported. Static analysis checks code you WROTE. Dynamic analysis runs the application and watches it behave.

items.objective: 4.3 Explain various activities associated with vulnerability management.
items.stem: A team decides not to patch a legacy system, documents the business justification, obtains sign-off and adds network restrictions instead. Which two 4.3 responses are in play?
options: Exceptions and exemptions, plus compensating controls
items.explanation: The documented decision not to patch is an exception/exemption; the network restrictions standing in for the patch are a compensating control. Both are named 4.3 vulnerability responses.

items.objective: 4.3 Explain various activities associated with vulnerability management.
items.stem: After a patch is applied, the team runs the scanner again against the same host to confirm the finding no longer appears. Which validation activity is this?
items.explanation: Rescanning is the specific act of running the scanner again. Verification is the broader conclusion the objectives list alongside it, and audit is the independent check by someone else.

items.objective: 4.3 Explain various activities associated with vulnerability management.
items.stem: A threat intelligence source aggregates indicators from publicly available websites, forums and DNS records at no cost. Which feed type is this?
items.explanation: OSINT is drawn from public sources. An information-sharing organization is a members-only community such as an ISAC; proprietary feeds are commercial products you buy.

items.objective: 4.4 Explain security alerting and monitoring concepts and tools.
items.stem: A detection rule fires two thousand times a day on legitimate backup traffic. Analysts adjust its threshold and exclusions. Which activity is this?
items.explanation: Alert tuning changes the RULE so it stops producing noise. Quarantine acts on a FILE or host. Both appear under alert response and remediation, and questions turn on which object is being changed.

items.objective: 4.4 Explain security alerting and monitoring concepts and tools.
items.stem: Which tool provides a standardised, machine-readable way to express security configuration checks so scanners from different vendors can consume them?
items.explanation: SCAP is the FORMAT. A benchmark is CONTENT expressed in that format. The stem asks about interoperability between tools, which is a property of the format.

items.objective: 4.4 Explain security alerting and monitoring concepts and tools.
items.stem: A monitoring system records summarised metadata about every conversation on the network — source, destination, ports, bytes — but not the contents. Which tool is this?
items.explanation: NetFlow is metadata about conversations. A packet capture (4.9) holds the payload. "But not the contents" is the discriminator.

items.objective: 4.4 Explain security alerting and monitoring concepts and tools.
items.stem: A network device sends an unsolicited alert to the management station the moment an interface goes down. Which mechanism is this?
items.explanation: A trap is DEVICE-INITIATED — the device speaks without being asked. Ordinary SNMP polling is the manager asking. The word "unsolicited" is the tell.

items.objective: 4.4 Explain security alerting and monitoring concepts and tools.
items.stem: Logs from firewalls, servers and applications are collected into one platform where they are normalised and correlated to raise alerts. Which tool is this?
items.explanation: A SIEM aggregates and CORRELATES across sources. Log aggregation alone would collect them; the correlation and alerting is what makes it a SIEM.

items.objective: 4.4 Explain security alerting and monitoring concepts and tools.
items.stem: An organisation must retain security logs for seven years but only needs the last 90 days searchable. Which monitoring activity covers the older data?
items.explanation: Archiving is the named 4.4 activity for long-term retention of data you are no longer actively querying. It is the activity most often forgotten when reproducing the list.

items.objective: 4.5 Given a scenario, modify enterprise capabilities to enhance security.
items.stem: A domain owner publishes a DNS record listing which mail servers are permitted to send mail for that domain. Which email security mechanism is this?
options: Domain-based Message Authentication Reporting and Conformance (DMARC)
items.explanation: SPF authorises the SENDING SERVER. DKIM signs the MESSAGE. DMARC is the policy on top saying what to do when either fails. This three-way split is tested every sitting.

items.objective: 4.5 Given a scenario, modify enterprise capabilities to enhance security.
items.stem: A domain owner publishes a policy instructing receiving servers to quarantine mail that fails authentication, and to send aggregate reports back. Which mechanism is this?
options: Domain-based Message Authentication Reporting and Conformance (DMARC)
items.explanation: Only DMARC carries a POLICY and a REPORTING address. SPF and DKIM produce results; DMARC decides what those results mean and tells you about them.

items.objective: 4.5 Given a scenario, modify enterprise capabilities to enhance security.
items.stem: A resolver refuses to return an address for domains on a malicious-domain list, so clients cannot reach them. Which capability is this?
items.explanation: DNS filtering blocks the LOOKUP, before any connection is attempted. A web filter inspects the HTTP request itself and can categorise the page — it needs the connection to exist.

items.objective: 4.5 Given a scenario, modify enterprise capabilities to enhance security.
items.stem: An agent computes a hash of critical system binaries hourly and alerts when one changes unexpectedly. Which capability is this?
items.explanation: FIM watches specific files for CHANGE. EDR watches BEHAVIOUR and can respond. The stem describes hashing and comparison, not behavioural analysis.

items.objective: 4.5 Given a scenario, modify enterprise capabilities to enhance security.
items.stem: A system blocks an email containing a spreadsheet of customer card numbers from leaving the organisation. Which capability is this?
items.explanation: DLP inspects data in motion, at rest or in use against content rules and blocks exfiltration. The trigger here is the CONTENT of the attachment, which is DLP's defining behaviour.

items.objective: 4.5 Given a scenario, modify enterprise capabilities to enhance security.
items.stem: A platform flags an accountant who suddenly begins accessing engineering file shares at 03:00, behaviour unlike their own history. Which capability is this?
items.explanation: UBA baselines an individual against THEIR OWN history. A SIEM correlates events across sources but does not inherently model one person's normal behaviour.

items.objective: 4.5 Given a scenario, modify enterprise capabilities to enhance security.
items.stem: Windows workstations receive their security settings centrally from Active Directory, and local changes are reverted at the next refresh. Which mechanism is this?
items.explanation: Group Policy is the named 4.5 operating system security mechanism for Windows; SELinux is its Linux counterpart in the same bullet. Configuration enforcement is the generic 2.5 mitigation.

items.objective: 4.5 Given a scenario, modify enterprise capabilities to enhance security.
items.stem: A device is denied network access until it proves it has current antivirus signatures and an approved OS patch level. Which capability is this?
items.explanation: NAC adds POSTURE ASSESSMENT — checking the device's health, not just its identity. 802.1X (3.2) authenticates the device at the port; NAC decides based on its state.

items.objective: 4.5 Given a scenario, modify enterprise capabilities to enhance security.
items.stem: An IDS is configured to alert when traffic matches a known pattern for a specific exploit. Which detection method is this?
items.explanation: Signatures match KNOWN patterns and cannot see novel attacks. Trends (anomaly) compare against a baseline and can, at the cost of false positives. The objectives list both under IDS/IPS.

items.objective: 4.5 Given a scenario, modify enterprise capabilities to enhance security.
items.stem: A web filter blocks a site because the destination has a poor score derived from its history of hosting malware. Which web filter feature is this?
items.explanation: Reputation is a score derived from HISTORY. Content categorization sorts a site by TOPIC — gambling, social media. Both can block the same site for different reasons.

items.objective: 4.6 Given a scenario, implement and maintain identity and access management.
items.stem: Access to classified files is determined by the system comparing the file's label to the user's clearance. Neither the user nor the file owner can override it. Which model is this?
items.explanation: Mandatory: the SYSTEM decides by label and nobody can override. Discretionary: the DATA OWNER decides and can grant access at will. The phrase "cannot override" is the tell.

items.objective: 4.6 Given a scenario, implement and maintain identity and access management.
items.stem: Permissions are assigned to job functions such as "AP Clerk" and users inherit them by being placed in that function. Which model is this?
items.explanation: Role is about WHO the person is — their job. Rule is a condition the system evaluates regardless of who they are. Both abbreviate to RBAC, and the acronym list carries both entries.

items.objective: 4.6 Given a scenario, implement and maintain identity and access management.
items.stem: Access is granted only if the user is in the finance department, on a managed device, and connecting from a corporate network. Which model is this?
items.explanation: Attribute-based combines multiple properties of subject, object and environment. A single blanket condition applied to everyone would be rule-based; three combined properties is ABAC.

items.objective: 4.6 Given a scenario, implement and maintain identity and access management.
items.stem: Before issuing credentials, an organisation checks a new joiner's passport and employment records to confirm they are who they claim. Which process is this?
items.explanation: Proofing happens ONCE at enrolment and establishes that the identity is real. Authentication happens at every subsequent login and only proves the same person is back.

items.objective: 4.6 Given a scenario, implement and maintain identity and access management.
items.stem: A university lets students sign in to an external research portal using their university credentials, with the university asserting their identity. Which concept is this?
items.explanation: SSO is one login across systems YOU own. Federation crosses an ORGANISATIONAL boundary and requires a trust relationship between the two parties.

items.objective: 4.6 Given a scenario, implement and maintain identity and access management.
items.stem: Which protocol is designed to grant a third-party application delegated authorisation to a resource without sharing the user's password?
items.explanation: OAuth grants delegated AUTHORISATION. SAML carries authentication ASSERTIONS between an identity provider and a service provider. The word "authorization" is inside the OAuth acronym for a reason.

items.objective: 4.6 Given a scenario, implement and maintain identity and access management.
items.stem: An administrator requests elevated rights, which are granted automatically for 30 minutes and then removed. Which PAM tool is this?
items.explanation: Just-in-time is about the TIME the permission exists. Password vaulting is about checking a shared credential in and out. Ephemeral credentials are secrets that expire after use.

items.objective: 4.6 Given a scenario, implement and maintain identity and access management.
items.stem: A shared administrator password is held in a central store, checked out for a session, then automatically rotated. Which PAM tool is this?
items.explanation: Vaulting is about custody of a CREDENTIAL — checked out, then rotated. Just-in-time is about the duration of a PERMISSION. The rotation after checkout is the vaulting tell.

items.objective: 4.6 Given a scenario, implement and maintain identity and access management.
items.stem: A user authenticates with a password and a code from a hardware token. Which two factors are in use?
options: Something you know and something you have
Something you know and something you are
Something you have and somewhere you are
Something you are and something you have
items.explanation: A password is knowledge; a token is a physical object. Biometrics would be "something you are", and location would be "somewhere you are" — the fourth factor the objectives list.

items.objective: 4.6 Given a scenario, implement and maintain identity and access management.
items.stem: Managers are required each quarter to review and confirm that their staff still need the access they hold. Which 4.6 term describes this?
items.explanation: Attestation is confirming that an identity or entitlement is still valid. Proofing establishes the identity at the start; attestation re-confirms the entitlement later.

items.objective: 4.6 Given a scenario, implement and maintain identity and access management.
items.stem: When an employee leaves, an automated workflow disables their accounts and revokes group memberships within minutes. Which 4.6 activity is this?
items.explanation: The objectives pair provisioning and de-provisioning of user accounts. De-provisioning is the leaver half, and its absence is exactly what makes the dismissed-administrator scenario possible.

items.objective: 4.7 Explain the importance of automation and orchestration related to secure operations.
items.stem: A deployment pipeline automatically refuses to apply any configuration that would open a storage bucket to the public internet. Which use case does the objectives document name?
items.explanation: Guard rails constrain what an automated process is ALLOWED to do. Security groups are the access grouping being managed. Enforcing baselines is a benefit, not a use case.

items.objective: 4.7 Explain the importance of automation and orchestration related to secure operations.
items.stem: A SOC automates tier-one triage so three analysts handle the alert volume that previously needed nine. Which benefit does the objectives document name?
items.explanation: Workforce multiplier is about HEADCOUNT capacity — the same people covering more. Efficiency/time saving is about the clock on an individual task. The stem is explicitly about staff numbers.

items.objective: 4.7 Explain the importance of automation and orchestration related to secure operations.
items.stem: Years of quick fixes in an automation platform now make every change slow and risky. Which 4.7 consideration is this?
items.explanation: Technical debt is what PAST shortcuts cost you later. Complexity is what the system is like NOW. The stem's "years of quick fixes" points at accumulated debt.

items.objective: 4.7 Explain the importance of automation and orchestration related to secure operations.
items.stem: An organisation automates account creation so that a new hire's accounts, groups and mailbox are created from the HR record. Which use case is this?
items.explanation: User provisioning creates ACCOUNTS. Resource provisioning creates INFRASTRUCTURE — servers, storage, network. The objectives list both separately and the object being created is the discriminator.

items.objective: 4.7 Explain the importance of automation and orchestration related to secure operations.
items.stem: A team automates its entire alert pipeline through one orchestration platform. What risk does the objectives document specifically name for this?
items.explanation: Concentrating everything in one platform makes that platform a single point of failure — named explicitly among the 4.7 "other considerations" alongside complexity, cost, technical debt and supportability.

items.objective: 4.8 Explain appropriate incident response activities.
items.stem: Ransomware is actively encrypting file shares. The team disconnects the affected servers from the network. Which incident response phase is this?
items.explanation: Containment limits SPREAD while the threat is still present. Eradication REMOVES it. Order matters: you contain before you eradicate, and "patch the vulnerability" is wrong while the attack is live.

items.objective: 4.8 Explain appropriate incident response activities.
items.stem: The malware has been removed and systems verified clean. The team now restores data and returns services to production. Which phase is this?
